strengths: The paper identifies and formulates a practically relevant fine-grained non-IID setting for federated learning, where knowledge is shared at global, subgroup, and client-specific levels.

The proposed FeMAM architecture is intuitive: it composes personalized predictions additively from models at multiple levels and progressively adds/prunes levels to adapt to heterogeneous client structures.

The empirical study is extensive across Tiny ImageNet and CIFAR-100 under multiple synthetic non-IID partitions, and the reported gains over clustered/personalized FL baselines are often large (e.g., 65.30% vs 58.83% on Tiny ImageNet multi-level).

The ablation and visualization analyses attempt to isolate the contribution of different levels and show that the learned multi-level structure can recover cluster boundaries/prune redundant levels in synthetic setups.
The paper includes convergence analysis and a cost discussion in the appendix, which are useful starting points for a structured FL method.
weaknesses: The convergence analysis is not sound for the proposed algorithm or the experiments: it assumes convex and Lipschitz-smooth losses, while all experiments use deep nonconvex ResNet-9 models. The learning-rate condition in Theorem 2 can become negative/unimplementable because of the term (||...||^2 - BU^2)/(||...||^2 + sigma^2), and the proof ignores progressive level addition, pruning, and fixed-number clustering. The main text condition also uses parameter norms while the proof uses gradient norms, showing internal inconsistency.

The objective and algorithm are not aligned. Eq. (3)/(5) assign every client one model at every level, but Algorithm 1 can remove an intermediate model and continue to later levels, creating non-contiguous and variable-length pathways that are not reflected in the additive objective. It is also unclear whether cluster-level predictions use the local model theta_i^{(l)} or the broadcast cluster centroid Theta_{C_l(i)}^{(l)} at inference.

The claim of approximating arbitrary multi-level non-IID structure is weakened by fixing the number of clusters per level (K_l=5) and the maximum number of levels (L=5). The ground-truth synthetic partitions have 9, 15, and 22 clusters, and the authors themselves state that FeMAM is not expected to recover them because K is fixed. Thus the method does not actually learn the cluster cardinality structure.

The multi-level non-IID setting is synthetic and not formally defined beyond class-split examples; there are no real-world federated datasets with natural hierarchical client structure. As a result, the significance of the proposed setting and the generality of the empirical results are limited.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code link ('Our code is available at' is blank), and the paper contains many presentation/formatting errors ('Mazro-F1', 'FemMAM', 'Clien-wise', missing references, unclear symbols). The baseline tuning and fairness are also unclear, especially since FeMAM uses validation-guided pruning while some baselines may not receive equivalent structure/model selection.

The pruning criterion uses validation loss with epsilon=0, while the same validation set is used for checkpoint selection, creating potential overfitting/selection bias in the reported structure discovery. The paper also does not analyze the privacy or communication implications of storing and combining multiple level models per client.

The experimental comparison omits the closely related clustered additive modeling work [34] and relies on synthetic class partitions, so it is difficult to assess whether the gains come from the multi-level formulation or simply from additional models/levels and validation-based model selection.

strengths: The multi-level non-IID framing is intuitive and well-motivated: decomposing knowledge into global/cluster/personalized levels offers a clean conceptual picture (Fig. 1) of a real FL problem that prior work only handles in special cases.

The qualitative structure-discovery result is genuinely interesting: Fig. 4 and Fig. A.1 show that the learned level-wise assignments and pruning recover the ground-truth cluster boundaries, which is a compelling piece of evidence that the method can adapt to some hidden structure.

The empirical study is broad in scope—two datasets (Tiny ImageNet, CIFAR-100), three non-IID families plus IID, many baselines (FedAvg, FedProx, pFedMe, Ditto, FedRep, FeSEM, local), mean±std over 4 runs, and Macro-F1 alongside accuracy.

The practical engineering choices (progressive level addition, freezing previous levels, pruning models whose validation-loss reduction is below ε) are sensible and explained clearly, and the 'No Free Lunch' appendix (App. A) gives an honest treatment of added storage/compute cost.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is thin. The realized architecture is simply an additive stack of existing components: Level 1 = FedAvg, Levels 2..L-1 = FeSEM (clustered FL), Level L = local training. The additive/residual composition itself was already explored in [18], [35], and most directly [34] (clustered additive modeling). The closest prior work [34] and the other additive works are cited but never compared empirically, so the marginal contribution over clustered additive modeling is not established.

The convergence analysis does not support the claims as stated. Assumption D.3 requires the local loss to be convex, which is incompatible with the ResNet-9 models actually used. Theorem 2's learning-rate condition depends on ||∇ℓ||², on the gradient bound U, and on the distance to cluster centroids—none of which can be checked a priori—so 'R decreases monotonically when this η condition holds' is essentially a tautological condition on the step size rather than a useful convergence guarantee. Theorem 1's bound is likewise circular (it is the very quantity that must shrink). No convergence rate is provided.

The central evaluation setting is constructed to match the method. The 'multi-level non-IID' partition splits classes into a global level, then clusters, then personalized levels—exactly FeMAM's global→cluster→personalized architecture. Strong performance here does not demonstrate the claimed ability to 'approximate arbitrary structures of non-IID'; it demonstrates fitting a data-generation process that mirrors the model. The claim of handling 'arbitrary' structure is therefore overstated.

The claim of 'jointly learning models and structure' (contribution bullet 3) is inconsistent with the actual algorithm: Algorithm 1 trains each level to convergence before adding the next, and the number of clusters K_l is fixed to 5 at every cluster level. Only the assignment and the pruning are adaptive, so 'automatically optimizing the knowledge-sharing structure' is a significant overstatement of the method's adaptivity.

Evidence/reporting problems: Table 1 appears internally inconsistent (e.g., the value 60.46±0.35 and 33.29±0.15 recur in mismatched rows/columns, and rows are misaligned), which undermines confidence in reproducibility. No significance testing is reported even though several margins over the best baseline (e.g., Ditto on multi-level) are only a few points. The code link is missing ('available at'), and Table C.1 with the data-partition definitions is garbled.

Baseline coverage is uneven in the main results: FedProx and FedRep are relegated to the appendix even though the main table claims a comprehensive comparison, and no additive-modeling competitor (the most relevant class of methods) is included in any table, making the 'surpasses existing clustered FL and personalized FL' claim weaker than presented.

Presentation quality is low throughout: recurring typos and naming inconsistencies (e.g., 'Clien-wise', 'FeAvg', 'PFedMe' vs 'pFedMe', 'Mazro-F1' for Macro-F1, 'Lipschitz Dmooth', 'Covergence'), an unsigned/placeholder code link, and a table-caption/appendix rendering problem (the IID curve is labeled Fig. 3(d) but placed after 3(c)).

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and intuitive multi-level additive modeling framework that naturally integrates global, clustered, and personalized knowledge in federated learning, with progressive level addition and pruning to discover client-specific model pathways.

Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet across cluster-wise, client-wise, multi-level, and IID partitions show consistent and often large improvements over clustered/personalized FL baselines; ablations and structure visualizations provide useful qualitative evidence for the multi-level design.

The practical implementation is well motivated: progressive level addition, freezing previous levels, and validation-based pruning make the method more stable and communication-efficient, and the appendix discusses the no-free-lunch trade-offs in computation, memory, and inference.

Code is available, and the empirical protocol includes multiple non-IID settings, several baselines, repeated runs with mean/std, and supplementary accuracy curves and multi-level structure visualizations.
weaknesses: The convergence analysis is not convincing. It assumes convexity and bounded gradients, uses learning-rate conditions that depend on current gradient norms in an unusual way, and does not establish a meaningful convergence rate for the nonconvex deep networks used in the experiments. The theory also does not match the progressive greedy training algorithm actually used.

The technical novelty is incremental. The method is essentially sequential additive stacking of FedAvg, FeSEM-style clustered models, and local personalized models, closely related to prior clustered additive modeling. No simple additive ensemble baseline is compared to isolate the benefit of the proposed dynamic level learning and pruning.

The evaluation may favor FeMAM. The synthetic multi-level non-IID partition mirrors the proposed hierarchy, cluster levels are fixed to K=5 even when ground-truth multi-level structures have varying cluster counts, and baselines are not given comparable multi-level capacity. Parameter-space K-means clustering is also questionable for neural network models due to permutation and scale sensitivity.

Reproducibility and presentation have issues: the validation-set description is inconsistent ('half of the original testing set' vs 'split from the original training set'), details on seeds and per-level communication rounds are incomplete, and the manuscript contains typos/mislabeling such as 'FemMAM' and contradictory runtime wording. Pruning with epsilon=0 based on validation loss may also be noisy and is not statistically characterized.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: multi-level, structured non-IID heterogeneity in federated learning, moving beyond fixed cluster counts or fixed global-plus-local personalization.
The proposed additive residual composition across multiple levels is simple and intuitive, and the grow-and-prune mechanism enables client-specific personalization depth and resource adaptivity.
The framework is flexible: it can instantiate different FL methods at different levels (e.g., FedAvg, K-means clustered FL, local training), which is demonstrated in the experimental instantiation.

The empirical evaluation is extensive for the simulated setting: two benchmark datasets, three non-IID partitions, strong clustered/personalized baselines, 4 runs with mean/std, ablations on L and K, and cost/efficiency analyses.

Results generally support the main empirical claim: FeMAM outperforms representative baselines across most non-IID settings (e.g., Tiny ImageNet multi-level 65.30 vs 59.11 for pFedMoE), and Fig. 5 shows client-specific depth adapts to heterogeneity.
The paper includes a foundation-model LoRA experiment on task-partitioned FLAN-T5 tasks, showing FeMAM also improves ROUGE-1/loss in a contemporary setting, albeit at modest scale.
Limitations are discussed honestly, including the narrow exploration of level-wise FL methods and the relatively small large-scale evaluation.
No material ethical concerns are evident; the work is privacy-preserving and the authors declare no financial conflicts of interest.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is not fully convincing. The convergence guarantee in Eq. (8)/D.18 relies on Assumption D.5, a boosting-edge/residual-alignment condition that essentially assumes the new level is sufficiently aligned with the residual it is supposed to correct. There is no empirical verification of gamma_l or of Assumptions D.3-D.5, so the claimed convergence analysis is conditional and does not establish convergence for the practical algorithm.

There is a theoretical mismatch between structure pruning and the objective used in the analysis. Pruning accepts a level if validation error decreases, whereas R_l in Appendix D is defined over the training objective. The monotonicity argument R_l <= R_{l-1} therefore does not follow unless validation and training losses coincide, which is not shown.

The novelty is incremental relative to existing additive FL and multi-level FL work (e.g., Agarwal et al. 2020; FedCAM/Ma et al. 2023; Kim et al. 2022; Guo et al. 2024). The main new elements are stacking multiple additive models and growing/pruning levels, which are natural extensions rather than a fundamental conceptual advance.

The adaptivity claim is somewhat overstated. In the main experiments, the hierarchy is fixed at L=5 with K=5 for intermediate levels and 50 for the final level. The method selects among pre-specified levels rather than discovering an unknown hierarchy from data; Table 3 shows robustness to K but does not demonstrate true structure discovery.

Important implementation details are missing for reproducibility. The initialization of the current level when it is added to frozen previous levels is not specified, which is critical for additive residual training. Algorithm 1 places assignment updates under server updates, but Eq. (5) uses local validation loss; the instantiated K-means assignment uses distance to centroids, creating ambiguity about whether assignments are client-side or server-side.

The experimental comparison has some gaps. Baseline hyperparameters are only briefly described, there are no statistical significance tests despite 4 runs, and some baseline results are surprisingly low or inconsistent (e.g., PM-MoE 27.37 on Tiny ImageNet cluster-wise; FedEM 37.34 vs FeMAM 65.30 on Tiny ImageNet multi-level), raising questions about tuning fairness.

The foundation-model experiment is small-scale: one base model (Qwen3-4B with LoRA), one task suite from LoraHub/FLAN-T5, 71 clients, 100 rounds, and no standard deviations or significance tests reported. The gains are modest (e.g., ROUGE-1 59.25 vs 58.65 for FeSEM), so the large-scale claim is weakly supported.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Eq. (6) is poorly formatted, the Algorithm 1 line references for pruning are incorrect (structure pruning is line 15, not lines 11-12), and there are typos/grammar issues such as 'FeMAM's can effectively adapt' and 'Numerica:'.

strengths: The multi-level non-IID formulation is well motivated: global, subgroup, and client-specific granularities are a realistic abstraction for modern federated personalization, and the smartphone example makes the problem intuitive.

The level-wise training/communication design is sensible: activating only one level per round keeps per-round communication comparable to single-model FL, and client-side pruning supports client-dependent personalization depth.

The empirical study covers several non-IID partitions (cluster-wise, Dirichlet client-wise, synthetic multi-level), includes IID, and reports ablations for L and K plus a foundation-model/LoRA case study.
The paper shows that learned depths align with heterogeneity level in the simulated experiments (Figures 4 and 5), which qualitatively supports the adaptive-depth argument.
The limitations section is relatively honest about the narrow instantiation and limited large-scale evaluation, and there are no obvious research-ethics concerns for the public datasets used.
weaknesses: The convergence analysis does not support the central theoretical claim. The cross-level monotone-descent result (Eqs. D.17-D.18) relies on Assumption D.5, which essentially assumes that the newly trained level is sufficiently aligned with the residual; this is not proved and is a strong, untested condition. The within-level bound is a standard local-SGD result and is not specific to FeMAM.

The analysis conflates training and validation objectives. Structure pruning in Eq. (7) is based on validation loss, while R_l and Eq. (4) concern training loss. Thus the claim that pruning guarantees R_l <= R_{l-1} is not justified without explicitly assuming validation and training objectives coincide.

The method is an incremental combination of existing ideas: clustered additive modeling (Ma et al., 2023), boosting/residual learning, and validation-based early stopping. The grow-and-prune mechanism is simple validation gating rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm.

No controlled ablation isolates the benefit of multi-level additive composition from increased capacity/ensembling. FeMAM uses five levels, stores up to 66 server-side models in the instantiation, and includes a per-client local model; comparing against baselines with at most five shared models is not an equal-capacity comparison. The K-ablation results also suggest the final local level may dominate.

The paper does not compare against prior multi-level or hierarchical FL methods (e.g., Kim et al. 2022; Guo et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2024), despite positioning itself as a multi-level FL framework. This makes it difficult to assess the advance over existing multi-level approaches.

The empirical gains are not uniformly convincing. On CIFAR-100 cluster-wise, FeMAM (53.72±0.29) barely exceeds FedCAM (53.29±0.69). On the foundation-model tasks, ROUGE-1 is 59.25 vs. 58.65 for FeSEM and 58.00 for FedCAM, with no standard deviations or significance testing reported. The large-scale improvement is marginal and may be within noise.

The 'large-scale' evaluation is small and under-specified: 71 short tasks, LoRA rank 4, 100 rounds, no foundation-model-specific baselines, no variance, and an apparent mismatch between using Qwen3-4B as the base model and FLAN-T5-derived tasks. It does not convincingly demonstrate contemporary large-scale FL.

The adaptivity claim is overstated. K is fixed at 5, the maximum L is pre-set, and levels are manually assigned types (FedAvg/K-means/local). FeMAM does not discover the number of clusters or the hierarchy structure; it only prunes depth per client. Thus the claim of requiring less prior knowledge about task boundaries is only partially supported.

No significance tests or paired comparisons are reported. Four runs help, but many reported differences have overlapping standard deviations or no variance at all, so the 'consistently outperforms' claim is not statistically established.

The cost analysis is incomplete. Server-side storage and maintenance of many models are not analyzed; total communication across sequential levels may be higher than single-level baselines, yet no communication-volume numbers are given in Figure 7b. Inference memory can also be L-fold, mitigated only by parallel execution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The code link is not visible in the manuscript, and baseline hyperparameter/tuning details are sparse. A reader would struggle to reproduce all baselines exactly from the provided text.

Presentation has issues: Eq. (6) is malformed, notation is inconsistent (e.g., D_i, X_i, Y_i, script-L), there are typos such as 'Numerica', and some figure text is hard to read. These issues hinder clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: multi-level non-IID federated learning, where client similarity has global, subgroup, and client-specific structure. The smartphone/OS/app/activity motivating example is intuitive.

The proposed FeMAM framework is flexible and well motivated: it learns a hierarchy of additive residual components and lets clients compose personalized predictors across levels without pre-specifying hierarchy depth or cluster boundaries.

The level-wise boosting-style training and client-side pruning are simple, cost-aware, and communication-friendly: only the current level is trained/communicated per round, while previous levels remain frozen.

The empirical study is extensive. It includes CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet under cluster-wise, client-wise, and explicitly multi-level non-IID partitions, plus a contemporary foundation-model setting using Qwen3-4B with LoRA on FLAN tasks.
FeMAM generally outperforms strong clustered, personalized, and multi-model FL baselines across settings, with particularly large gains under client-wise and multi-level non-IID heterogeneity.

Ablations on hierarchy depth L and cluster count K, together with convergence curves, model-count distributions, and inference-storage analysis, provide useful evidence for the adaptive grow-and-prune behavior.
The paper includes a limitations section that honestly discusses the limited exploration of alternative level-wise components and the relatively small scale of the foundation-model evaluation.
Ethical concerns appear minimal: the work is privacy-preserving FL, includes a conflict-of-interest statement, and the impact statement is appropriately modest.
weaknesses: The theoretical convergence analysis is not fully convincing. The main bound in Eq. (8) relies on Assumption D.5, which essentially assumes that the newly added level is sufficiently aligned with the residual; this is close to assuming the boosting improvement rather than proving it. The resulting guarantee therefore does not establish convergence for the proposed training procedure in a practically meaningful sense.

Several assumptions in Appendix D are strong and not empirically validated. For example, Assumption D.3 bounds each client gradient deviation by a constant times the norm of the average gradient, which is restrictive and can imply very strong behavior when the average gradient is near zero. Assumption D.4 treats assignment updates abstractly with bounded slack, again limiting the force of the convergence claim.

The novelty is moderate. Additive modeling, clustered additive FL, and multi-level FL ideas already exist; FeMAM mainly combines them into a multi-level grow-and-prune pipeline. The grow-and-prune mechanism is mostly level-wise pruning per client rather than discovery of a fully general hierarchical structure.

The assignment and pruning procedures are heuristic. Eq. (5) selects models via a criterion that may not align with the true composed objective, and pruning uses local validation loss. With only a small per-client validation set (e.g., 5000 total validation examples over 50 clients in the image experiments), this decision can be noisy, and the claim that added levels are 'always utility-improving' is validation-dependent rather than test-utility guaranteed.

The experimental comparisons do not fully isolate the benefit of FeMAM's specific additive/grow-prune design. There is no ablation removing structure pruning while keeping all levels, nor a direct comparison between additive composition and alternative multi-level fusion mechanisms such as gating or concatenation. Some gains are marginal, e.g., cluster-wise Tiny ImageNet is essentially tied with FedCAM.

Some implementation details are underspecified, including behavior when a cluster receives no client assignments, how empty or unused level-wise models are handled in aggregation, and how the assignment criterion interacts with the frozen lower-level outputs over rounds.

Reproducibility is only partially demonstrated. The appendix provides substantial hyperparameter and task detail, but the provided manuscript shows a 'Code:' placeholder without a visible repository link, so independent reproduction cannot be verified from the submission alone.

There are minor presentation issues: Algorithm 1's text references 'line 11 and 12' for pruning even though those lines do not correspond to the described pruning step, and some notation in the assignment/objective equations is somewhat loose.
